items.body:
While `peer_schemas` is being assigned here and the versioning machinery treats it correctly, it's apparently not being sent by the syft-client, since `JobClient` is initialized using `.from_config` and there's no `peer_schemas` being passed anywhere.

The test cases are correct and pass `peer_schemas`, but the actual code doesn't.
Shouldn't `ref.job_name` be added to `extra` here too, since it comes from the path like `submitted_by` and `datasite_email`?
This will raise an error with jobs with the same name across protocol versions. Is that intended?
Blanket exception catches on a long block like this are an anti-pattern. It should catch specific exceptions, or at least log the error with the job name and path.
Since `receive_job` is only called by `scan_inbox`, which already determines the correct `protocol_version` on load, it should be required parameter, not default to the constant.

Won't a job have both `config.yaml` and `state.yaml` files after `scan_inbox` and `receive_job` are called, therefore `total_jobs` here is counting those jobs twice?

It doesn't affect deletion, since it uses `shutil.rmtree` but the warning message below will be misleading.
`JobManager.read_state` can return `None` if the `state.yaml` no longer exists. There should be a check here to prevent an exception on the `state.status` on the next line.

Both `_load_upgraded` and `_write_in_target_version` work for only two versions, but are somewhat fragile when it comes to handling more future versions, and specially once we need to upgrade or downgrade jobs throughout multiple versions.

Instead of conditionals I would introduce a `ProtocolCodec` class that handles the serialization and loading for each version, and `JobManager` delegates to the appropriate class, keeping all migration specific code in the codec class. Once v2 is introduced, it's just a new class, instead of more conditionals.
`JobManager` is a somewhat vague name that blurs the line with `JobClient`. Although the two have clearly distinct responsibilities, the suffix is not as clear. Maybe `JobRepository` or `JobStorage`.
Both `write_submission` and `write_state` could be renamed to make the asymmetry more explicit, like in the docstring. Like `write_submission_for_do` and `write_state_for_ds`.
`metadata.name` was replaced with `ref.job_name` in most places, but still remains in others like here.

The comments mark some minor issues found in the code.

The main high-level design issue would be having a separate `ProtocolCodec` class, to avoid bundling all protocol rules in the `_load_upgraded` and `_write_in_target_version` methods, as suggested in the comments.

items.body: The subpaths are defined below, but the prefixes are being imported from syft_datasets.dataset_manager. This comment seems contradictory.

Also, using a bare `except:` or a blanket `except Exception:` to silently suppress all errors is a python anti-pattern. In legitimate cases, `contextlib.suppress` is the more idiomatic way of doing that.

There's a lot of lines that violate encapsulation of the sync_engine's private attributes, most of them reaching into `self._sync._connection_router`.  If the goal of the refactoring is a "domain-free core", it should not reach into private internals. The sync_engine should have public methods exposing the functionality.
This method isn't honoring the `sync` parameter, like others do.

Redundant import. It's already imported at the top of the file.
Should be at the top too.

This checks if the file exists, but if it's empty, `yaml.safe_load` below returns `None`, causing an `AttributeError` on the `data.get` call next, that will  not interrupt flow, only be logged as a callback failure by the _emit handler . This is duplicating the construction logic that `SyftRDSClientConfig._compose` already does.
The `submit_bash_job` method above does not check peer-membership the same way this does. Was that intentional?
This should use `peer_manager.syncable_peers` instead of reaching inside `peer_store`, since the `syncable_peers` property exists for that.
This section is copy-paste from the `_upload_dataset_to_collection`. It should be extracted to a method to avoid code duplication.
This is also copy-paste from `upload_dataset_to_collection`.
This `PRE_SYNC` guard checking the env var is repeated three times. It should be extracted to a property, or maybe checked once and saved.

The word "sync" is carrying four different meanings in the file. That's a real readability issue. In most cases it refers to the `SyftboxManager` instance, but it's also used as a boolean flag meaning to run a full sync after the method, the `sync()` method itself, that delegates to `self._sync.sync()` , and `config.sync` referring to the sub-config.

I'd rename the boolean to something more explicit, like `sync_after`, and the private attribute to `_sync_engine` so it matches the public property `sync_engine`.

This interpolation is repeated four times in the file. It should be extracted to a common function/method.

Also, it's not clear why it assumes `collection_specs[0] ` is special.  Is it because it's the public spec? What happens if they are reordered? It should have a clarifying comment here.

If it must always be the public, it should refer to it by an unambiguous value.
The `sync` method calls `load_peers` on every invocation, so every `sync` emits `peers_loaded`. Is that intentional? Is there any idempotency handling?
Does this mean a peer added by the DO is approved automatically? If that's the case, there should be a comment clarifying it.
This is the same issue with the word "sync" mentioned in client.py. For clarity, the boolean could be renamed to `sync_after`.

The intent to create a domain-free core and define a public API is clear, but there are still violations of that boundary. It's mostly clear for the happy path, but there's still coupling and private-reaching when handling others cases.

title: feat: Validate and pin peer encryption bundles
author: rasswanth-s

items.body:
[blocker]

The pin comes only from `_peers`, and `set_peers()` replaces that list on every sync. If SYFT_peers.json marks Bob rejected for one sync, `load_peers()` and `get_peer_requests()` both drop him, and his in-memory pin is lost. On the next sync this line gives `pinned = None`, the first-use branch at 175 runs, and 182 writes the attacker's bundle over the pin in `crypto_keys.json`.

The same happens when Bob is in memory without a bundle while another process pinned him in the key file. When pinned is `None`, it fall back to the validated pin from the key file.

Something like this:

```
pinned = cached.public_encryption_bundle if cached else None
if pinned is None:
    pinned = self._valid_stored_pin(incoming.email)
```

I'd also add a test: pin Bob, sync with Bob rejected, sync with Bob accepted and a new key, then assert that the old pin stays and the warning appears.

[blocker]

`write_text()` is not safe for this. If the write crashes for any reason or the key file is corrupted, the next `load_keys()` fails, and the private keys can't be read back. It can also trigger the other issue, forcing `_stored_pin()` to treat the peer as a first use.

The repo already has `portalocker` as a dependency and solves this problem safely in `syft/sync/sync/caches/persisted_dict.py`. We should do the same atomic write here:

1. hold an exclusive lock over the read, change, and write.
2. write to a temp file, `fsync`, then `os.replace()` for an atomic modification.

[should fix]

The docstring says to run this once you have confirm the new fingerprint with the peer, but the call never sees that fingerprint. It adopts whatever bundle the storage servers. Since the storage provider is not fully trusted, this method should accept a fingerprint and raise an error when the published bundle does not match.

[should fix]

`from_did_document()` only ever raises `ValueError` for bad input. An error unrelated to the bundle that raises another error turns that into `InvalidPeerBundleError`, `load_keys()` drops every peer and the next sync trusts whatever Drive serves and falls back to first-use trust.

This bare `Exception` is bad, not just as a matter of style. A bug should fail loudly here for security reasons. It's part of the ticket.

[should fix]

This is similar to the blanket `Exception` in key_bundle.py:73. This turns every error into `no bundle`. This should catch the specific error possible here. HttpError, retriable network error, ValueError for most bad JSON errors.
@rasswanth-s The design is solid and the tests are good, but there are 2 blockers and 3 should-fix items.

title: feat(enclave): bind the enclave's encryption key into its attestation token
author: rasswanth-s

items.body:
[blocker]

With no `key_fingerprint`, this `caller_nonce` takes the fingerprint's slot at index 1, and the verifier later cannot tell which one built the token. A caller who sends their own fingerprint as the nonce gets a token signed by the provider, from the real image.

This should have a fixed placeholder at index 1 when `key_fingerprint` is `None`.

Something like this:

```python
NO_KEY_FINGERPRINT_NONCE = "syft-no-key"

def build_eat_nonce(
    caller_nonce: str | None = None, key_fingerprint: str | None = None
) -> list[str]:
    nonces = [f"syft-{syft.__version__}", key_fingerprint or NO_KEY_FINGERPRINT_NONCE]
    if caller_nonce:
        nonces.append(caller_nonce)
    return nonces
```

title: refactor: Added initial stub contracts
author: rasswanth-s

items.body: Mailbox here uses list->fetch->ack, but the v2 ticket replaces this with send->receive->ack->delivered. Maybe we can define the v2 shape now and move the callers only once, doing the list and fetch inside received.
Why do we have different behavior for PROPOSALS and EVENTS, in the same method? Can't both use the same rules from the start?

Why are we combining both peer registry, owner, and watcher in a single PrivateStore class, while OwnerStorage and WatcherStorage only forward each call here? It feels like there's an unnecessary layer here. With two OwnerStore and WatcherStore classes instead of a single PrivateStore, there's no need for the intermediary layer.

There's some redundancy in these event log methods. Three primitive methods are enough: `append_event`, `list_event_handles(since)` and `fetch(handle)`. The others can be concrete implementations on the base class instead of abstracts to be implemented by the concrete class.

- `fetch_all_events()` is `fetch_events_since(None)`
- `fetch_events_since(t)` is `fetch` for each handle from `list_event_handles(t)`.
- `count_events_since(t)` is `len(list_event_handles(t))`.
The v1 ticket has the peer registry methods in `PeeringConnection`. It's fine to be in `PrivateStore`, but the ticket should be updated to avoid confusion.
`list_mine` is `list_mine_with_permissions` without the flags. Keep one abstract, make the other a concrete helper.
`download` is `list_files` and `fetch_file` for each file. It could be a concrete helper, not abstract.
The name `PeerState` is already used by the enum at `syft.sync.peers.peer.PeerState`. The docstring warns about it, but it should have a different name.

This can read the key bundle of a peer, but it cannot read the bundle of this client. The auto encryption settings work (branch `pjwerneck/auto-encryption-settings`) adds `read_own_encryption_bundle` to the Drive connection. Please add `read_own_key_bundle(peer)` here, so the two branches merge without a change to the contract.
The ticket calls this `Connections` not `Transport`. Transport is a better name, but the ticket should be updated.

The ticket says: Lost view → PeerReset → resend everything. This docstring proposes that if no view exist, the tracker assumes that each peer already holds all files it can read.

This prevents a full resend after the upgrade, but a peer that does not have a file never gets it.

The ticket keeps the views on Drive when `persist_owner_state` is true. It adds `deliveries` and `peer_resets` to `RollingState` and `IncrementalCheckpoint`, and `peer_views` to `Checkpoint`. Deliveries also count toward the upload threshold of the rolling state.

This stub keeps the views only in a local file (line 32). Is persistence to Drive in v2, or later? If it is later, an enclave loses the views at each boot. Then it sends all files again to each peer, or it sends nothing, as decided for line 21.

Left a few comments. Main points:

1. The `Mailbox` contract has a shape that V2 replaces. A contract with the V2 shape now prevents a second rewrite of every caller.
2. `OwnerStorage` and `WatcherStorage` are wrappers that only forward calls to `PrivateStore`. Two abstract classes give the same separation with one less layer.
3. Some abstract methods are compositions of other methods. A small set of primitives, plus helper methods on the base class, makes a backend easier to write.
4. `DeliveryTracker` differs from the ticket on the first run and on persistence to Drive.

title: feat: negotiate encryption policy per peer
author: pjwerneck

items.body:
`_adopt_key_file()` and `_take_key_file()` take the keys and pins of a key file loaded into a second store, and return the pins set in memory before keys existed so they can be saved.

I have trouble understanding from the name what this does. The main usage seems to be in `PeerStore.create`, which creates stores and juggles information between them, but it just seems way too complicated for what it does. I think this should be simplified.

`PeerStore.create()` now builds a store, loads the key file into a second store, copies the policy, keys and pins across with `_adopt_key_file()`, and then rewrites the file with `_record_required_policy()`.

We are doing a lot of things in place in the create method, I feel like that may be overcomplicating things. Also, why does `_read_key_file` return a dict? That should be typed.

`_publish_bundle_to_new_encrypted_peers()` publishes our bundle to each encrypting peer once per process: `_bundle_published_for` is an in-memory set, and `_own_bundle_is_published()` reads the bundle back from Drive.

It is not super clear to me that one is the local cache and one is the Drive state. It also seems like this is quite slow, because we do it for every peer and it's not in parallel.

When an outbox message has to wait, its paths stay pending and every later message to that recipient waits too, so they go out in order on a later sync.

Maybe don't queue, but warn and forget?

`watcher_get_events_messages()` now reads outbox messages one by one through `watcher_read_events_message()`, stops at the first one that cannot be read yet, and swaps a plaintext message in an encrypting pair for an empty one.

This logic is hard to follow, add comments.

The enclave now always makes keys at attestation, so that an `optional` enclave's keys are bound to the report too.

The enclave should never be booted without encryption.

`encryption_policy` is `Optional` so that a version file written by an older syft, without the field, reads as `None` and the peer is treated as outdated.

I think we dont need to be backwards compatible for the upcoming release.

`get_own_version()` copies the peer store's current policy onto the cached `VersionInfo` on every call, because tests and the enclave replace the store after the first call.

This feels like a code smell. Are we doing something wrong here?

When the version file is missing, it is now created from the passed `version_info`, and otherwise still from `VersionInfo.current()`, which carries no policy.

Why do we have 2 code paths here, do we need that?
Not really part of this PR, but `ensure_keys` is a bit vague as a name. We should probably mention "own keys".

When the client is not `required` and has no keys, `_keep_pinned_bundle()` now ignores the bundle in the Drive copy of `SYFT_peers.json` and keeps only a bundle that was set locally.

I am not sure what this is but it's confusing me a lot. I am not sure if this logic is something we want in the first place, and given the logic, it also seems to be a confusing name.

`my_fingerprint()` and `peer_fingerprint()` now return a fingerprint whenever keys exist, instead of only when encryption is on.

What is this and why do we have it?

`_pin_published_bundle()` now warns and returns `None` on an unreadable peer bundle instead of raising.

Again, lots of tech debt here, need to investigate.

`set_version_loader()` lets `SyftboxManager` hand `PeerManager.load_peer_version()` to each router, so `_refresh_unknown_peer()` can re-read a peer's version file before a send.

Why do we need `set_version_loader`?

`peer_policy_known()`, `encryption_ready()`, `should_hold()` and `take_policy_reread()` are new `PeerStore` helpers that decide whether a send to a peer goes now, waits, or first re-reads the peer's version file.

Do we need this complexity?

`_send_outbox_message()` returns `False` when the message has to wait for encryption with the peer, and `True` when it is written or dropped because the recipient is not a peer.

Can we not just raise?

`_decrypt_or_wait()` verifies and decrypts a message, and returns `None` with a warning when the peer's messages cannot be read yet.

`_decrypt_or_wait` is a weird name, it doesn't reflect what it's doing.

`sync_down_parallel()` now stops at the first message that cannot be read yet and leaves the cursor before it, so later messages apply in order once it can be read.

This again does a lot of handling of scenarios we don't care about.

A peer whose version file has no `encryption_policy` runs an older syft: `is_outdated` marks it, and `SyftboxManager.sync()` skips it with a warning to upgrade.

No need for backwards compatibility, we can just assume the policy is there.

`check_key_file_policy()`, called at the start of every `sync()`, reads the key file as a dict and raises when it records `required` but this client started with another policy, e.g. because syft-bg made the datasite required.

This data should be typed. I also don't get why we are talking about "processes".

This checks that a version file from an older syft, without the policy field, parses with `encryption_policy` as `None`.

Delete.
This tests that a peer whose version file has no `encryption_policy` is skipped with an upgrade warning. Without backwards compatibility for older version files, this test can be deleted.
This tests that a key file written before the `encryption_policy` field reads as `required`. Without backwards compatibility for the upcoming release, this test can be deleted too.
This tests that an outbox message waiting on encryption stays pending and is sent by the next process. If we warn and forget instead of queueing, this test can be deleted.
The enclave should never run without encryption, so a test that sets the enclave to `off` can be deleted.
The `plaintext` case runs the enclave without encryption, which should never happen. This case can be deleted; `encrypted` and `negotiated` cover the enclave.

items.body: `download_events_message_by_id` is not being called by anyone, so the modification here lands in unused code.

This `else` clause feels fragile. Right now there's only PROPOSED_CHANGES and FILE_EVENTS. It should have an explicit elif for FILE_EVENTS and a warning for the else so it doesn't fail silently in case a new kind is added in the future,

Minor, but `get_events_count_since_checkpoint` counts every name that starts with syfteventsmessagev3_, while list_event_handles() drops names that don't parse. The contract says the count is `len(list_event_handles())`.

title: feat: delivery tracker - deliver owner changes from per-peer views
author: pjwerneck

items.body:
`sync()` now reloads the permissions, seeds the views, records local changes, delivers, and then pulls each peer's proposals, sending again after each pull.

I think it has gotten a little bit messy in terms of when what happens. A while ago, we would pull all the changes, check what happened locally, put that in the queue and then deliver from the queue. It feels like all of that is intertwined a little bit now. Why?

The owner's changes are now sent before the proposals are pulled, so that a proposal that raises (for example an outdated one) does not hold them back.

We can just ignore those proposal errors.

`sync()` first delivers the owner's changes, then pulls each peer's proposals, and the `process_syftbox_events_queue()` in that loop sends again.

I don't like the ordering of things. Why are we first delivering things, then pulling changes and delivering again, is that necessary? This doesn't help for reducing the number of API calls we want to make, because we don't batch things properly. It's also more confusing to follow. Also, `_record_local_changes` is a confusing name.

Rejecting a peer resets its view, so a later approval sends it every file it may read.

We should have an option for a peer to request all the files they can see. So if a peer lost their state they can kind of relogin.

The views are kept in `.cache/owner_delivery_views.json`, and every change loads and rewrites the whole file under a lock.

Ideally `owner_delivery_views` should be a sqlite and not a json (keep this very simple), so writes (and reads) are not costly. We should also keep an in-memory option for this.

`_seed_views_if_missing()` fills the views on the first sync after an upgrade, and marks the paths the old client listed in `owner_pending_deliveries.json` as unsent.

We don't need backwards compatibility for existing clients, so we can remove both the seeding (`_seed_views_if_missing()`, `_files_held_by_peer_at_seed()`, `DeliveryTracker.seed()` / `is_seeded()` and the `seeded` flag) and the reading of `owner_pending_deliveries.json` (`legacy_pending_paths()`), with the `test_upgrade_*` tests. Resending every file once after an upgrade is fine.

When the owner accepts a change from a peer, `accept()` records the other readers it is withheld from, so only the submitter gets it until the owner edits the file again.

Every peer with read permission should get the file.

When a send fails with anything other than a not-ready peer, the error is raised and the planned messages not yet sent are dropped; only unplanned messages go back on the queue.

I wonder whether this is a good idea if one broken message blocks the rest.

title: feat: delivery tracker - deliver owner changes from per-peer views
author: pjwerneck

items.body:
`_send_outbox_messages()` treats two kinds of message differently. Planned messages, which `deliver_file_changes()` builds from the views, are dropped on failure and planned again. Unplanned ones (the accepted change sent back to the submitter, dataset and enclave shares) are put back on the queue. Telling them apart takes the `planned` flag, the `not_ready` set and the `finally`.

I think we can handle both cases more simply, and the same way: every peer with read permission should get them, and for delivery we just try to deliver and requeue if it failed (but not indefinitely).

title: feat: release job outputs and logs through one path
author: pjwerneck

items.body:
`_prepare_outputs_dir()` now removes `outputs/` in both review/ and staging/ through `JobStorage.remove_outputs()`, then deletes the last run's `output_recipients.json` and `outputs_error.txt` from the job's staging folder one file at a time.

Why do we not remove the full staging dir, what is the reasoning?

After a run, the outputs are now copied into the job's `staging/outputs` instead of `review/outputs`, and only reach `review/` when they are released.

Isn't this confusing from a DO perspective? Let's say I ran a job, now I want to read files, but now the folder I am expecting is empty. Not sure if I am sold on this staging folder but perhaps we can discuss.
A `syft.pub.yaml` that a job writes into `outputs/` is now left out of the copy to staging, and the job fails. Before, it landed in `review/outputs` and its rules decided who could read the outputs.

`release()` takes one list of file names and one list of recipients, and grants every recipient read on every file.

This should ideally be a dict with filenames as keys and a list of recipients as values. This would be a flexible enough data structure to allow any kind of sharing.

`release_logs()` and `release_disclosures()` now both go through `release()`, which moves the files to review/ and grants read on them. `release_disclosures()` releases `granted_disclosures`, which is computed from the grant stored in `disclosures.json`.

I think release is a bit more confusing than "share", because release may also mean "make public" and "share" implies "with someone" a little bit more. Disclosures are just another name for read permissions, so let's be consistent and use that. Also I think it's weird that disclosures are stored in a file, that could be implied from the permissions so it's duplicate information that we need to keep in sync now. I think we just need 1) request read_permissions, 2) approval 3) actual read_permissions, from permissions files, anything else can be inferred. I also don't understand the difference between disclosures and granted_disclosures.

`JobInfo.share_outputs()` and `share_logs()` are gone: outputs now go out through `release(["outputs"], recipients)` and logs through `release_logs()`, while the public entry point stays `share_job_results()`.

Why do we have release_logs but not release_outputs? Also we have `release` at the low level now and `share` at the top level.

`_release_outputs()` sends the outputs through a read grant and the sync, but still pushes `state.yaml` to each recipient through the event outbox, because the DOs hold no read grant on it.

Wouldn't it make more sense to just give the DOs read access on `state.yaml` in the first place?

`write_receipt()`, `write_receipt_error()` and `_receipt()` now use `artifact_path("outputs")`, which is `staging/outputs` until the outputs are released.

Let's revert this when removing staging.

`_forward_new_releases()` and its `forwarded_artifacts.json` record are gone. An item the submitter requested and every DO granted, also after the run, is now released by `_apply_disclosure_policy()` through `release()`, and the sync delivers it.

The idea behind enclave disclosures was that 1) a DS (may be one of the DOs) submits a job 2) the job crashes 3) the DOs decide that they want to share the logs (or parts of it) and they still have a way to do this.

`setup_ds_job_folder_as_do()` sets up the DS's review folder through `review_grants.py: grant_ds_review_read()`, which gives the DS read on only `state.yaml` and `disclosures.json` in each job folder, and removes any read on the whole folder.

This is not the right place, but `grant_ds_review_read` is a weird function name, because it describes something it doesn't do.
